title: Metal Meets Orchestra: What It Actually Takes
body:
## Why Metal Bands Are Falling in Love With Real Orchestras

If you've spent any time in metal Facebook groups lately, you've probably seen the buzz around Septicflesh's new album, Modern Primitive. It's their eleventh record, and it's a big one: a full adult choir, a full children's choir, a symphony orchestra, plus instruments like duduk, santur, oud, and bouzouki woven right into the songs — not just sprinkled on top for effect. Blast beats and death growls sitting shoulder to shoulder with a children's choir. It sounds like it shouldn't work. It absolutely does.

## This Isn't a New Idea — It's Just Getting Bigger

Bands mixing heavy guitars with real orchestras isn't new. Septicflesh have been doing it since their 2008 comeback album Communion, largely thanks to Christos Antoniou, who writes their orchestral arrangements and also happens to hold a Master's degree in concert music. What's changed is the scale. Where a band might once have used a handful of strings or a sampled orchestra to add some atmosphere, albums like Modern Primitive go all in: full orchestra, full choir, and folk instruments that actually carry the melody, not just decorate it.

It's a good reminder that "orchestral metal" doesn't have to mean a cheesy string pad behind the riffs. Done properly, it's a real production — real players, real rooms, and real arranging work.

## So What Does "Recording an Orchestra" Actually Involve?

If you've never done this before, it can sound intimidating. It really isn't, once you break it down.

Someone has to turn the song into orchestral parts first. Most bands don't show up with a finished orchestral score — they show up with a demo, a rough MIDI mockup, or just an idea of where they want strings, brass, or choir to sit. That gets turned into real, playable sheet music for every instrument in the room.

Then you need real musicians in a room built for this. A metal mix and an orchestral recording want very different spaces. Distorted guitars and blast beats are close-mic'd and controlled; an orchestra and choir need a room with the right natural acoustics to sound huge and alive. Getting both to sit together in the final mix is a craft in itself.

Someone also has to manage a lot of moving parts — booking the right size ensemble (twenty players or eighty?), a conductor, a choir, the studio, and making sure everyone's parts are printed and ready before anyone plays a note. That's a full production job on its own, separate from writing the music.

And then it all has to blend. Brutal vocals, blast beats, and a children's choir don't naturally sit together in a mix without careful work. This is where a lot of home-recorded orchestral metal falls apart — not because the idea is bad, but because pulling it off cleanly takes real craft on the recording and mixing side.

## Why Prague, of All Places?

Here's a fun bit of trivia: Prague has quietly been one of the world's go-to cities for big orchestral recording for over 25 years, mostly known for film scores — Hollywood composers have been flying in since the '90s for exactly this kind of huge, cinematic sound. It's part of why so many "epic" soundtracks and, increasingly, symphonic metal albums end up tracing back to the same handful of studios and orchestras there. Septicflesh first teamed up with a Prague orchestra back on 2017's Codex Omega, and it's back again on Modern Primitive — a big part of why the album sounds as massive as it does.

## The Takeaway

Albums like Modern Primitive are a great reminder of what's possible when a band commits fully to the orchestral side of things instead of treating it as an afterthought. It's not about being a 25-year veteran act — it's about having the right players, the right room, and people who know how to make blast beats and a full choir sit together in one mix. When it comes together, it's one of the best sounds in metal, full stop.

title: Original Soundtrack | MAYA: Seed Takes Root | Trials of MAYA | Anand Gandhi & Zain Memon
body:
When it comes to bringing intimate, powerful, and nuanced musical arrangements to life, there's nothing quite like capturing a tight-knit ensemble playing together in real time.

We’re super excited to share a quick behind-the-scenes look at one of our recent recording projects featuring a 5-piece setup, which was coordinated and facilitated by MUSA.

Check out the full documentary-style session video below to see how this five-piece performance came together:

Whether it's for film, games, or standalone compositions, getting to capture this level of detail and synergy between a few top-tier players is always something special. Huge thanks to everyone who made this session happen!
